title: A saint's long darkness
hookLine: Mother Teresa's letters revealed decades without feeling God's presence, yet she kept going

lines: A WHITE SARI, A DYING MAN.
cards: A small woman in a white sari with blue stripes, bending over a dying man on a mat. Cameras followed her for years. She founded houses for the poor and the dying, spoke to presidents, and smiled in the photographs.
Catholics now call her Saint Teresa of Calcutta. After she died, her private letters to her spiritual directors were published. And in them, page after page, she describes darkness.
Emptiness. A God she couldn't feel. Prayer that seemed to go nowhere.
All the while, she kept getting up to pray, and going back to the mats.

teach.b: You met her in year three; this is what she kept hidden. She wrote of longing for God and not feeling him at all. Of a place in her soul that felt empty.
Of smiling on the outside while the inside felt like night. These were letters to the priests guiding her, and some she had hoped would stay private.
She kept going. The prayer, the chapel, the work with the sick, without the feeling that once carried her.
Her directors helped her see the darkness not as proof that God had left, but as part of following a Christ who himself cried out on the cross.
In her sisters' chapels, as their tradition keeps it, words of Jesus from the cross in John's Gospel are written beside the crucifix: "I thirst." The Bible has room for this.
Isaiah speaks to the one "that walketh in darkness, and hath no light," and says, "let him trust in the name of the LORD." Trust while it's dark. Paul writes, "For we walk by faith, not by sight."
And the prophet Habakkuk sings of a time when the fig tree doesn't blossom and the fields yield nothing: "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD." In spite of how it feels.
Some Christians assume that if God feels far away, something has gone wrong with their faith.
Her letters suggest another picture: faith can be a decision you keep making with your feet, when your feelings have gone quiet.

how: Catholics honor Mother Teresa as Saint Teresa of Calcutta, and her Missionaries of Charity keep a daily rhythm of prayer and service to the poor; some Christians of other churches read her letters too as encouragement to keep praying through seasons when God feels absent.

games.q: what does “a saint's long darkness” mean?
o: years of feeling no presence of God, while still praying
a punishment for a secret sin, kept from her sisters
a time a saint stopped believing and left her work

games.q: a saint's long darkness — tap the pairs.
p: darkness, emptiness, a God not felt
the fig tree fails, yet I will rejoice

s: Mother Teresa felt God's closeness all through her work
her private letters describe a long darkness and a God she could not feel.
she stopped praying when the feeling went away
she kept the prayer and the work going, without the feeling.
Paul writes that we walk by faith, not by sight
it's in his second letter to the Corinthians.

games.q: you're a nun who has given your life to the poor. for a long time, God feels completely absent when you pray. what do you do?
o: quit the order and go home.
keep praying and serving, and tell your spiritual director the truth.
pretend to everyone, including yourself, that it's fine.
games.why: the letters show she kept going, and told the priests guiding her exactly how dark it was. the honesty and the faithfulness went together.

practice: Think of one thing you've kept doing after it stopped feeling meaningful: a prayer, a visit, a promise, caring for someone. Just notice that you're still doing it, and let that count.

If you pray, pray as usual, even if nothing seems to come back; if you don't, simply stay with the breath. If the dark ever turns into thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: A saint's long darkness. Mother Teresa's hidden years of feeling no presence of God, kept company by prayer and work that never stopped.

carryVoice: Your line: faith without feeling. The week ran from a God who suffers to a saint in the dark. That's the week.
